extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in political science (especially those studying media effects and public opinion)
extracted.subtask_description: Concise summary of Iyengar & Kinder (1987) 'News that Matters' that outlines the book's main point and principal causal mechanisms (priming, framing, agenda-setting), with brief methodological notes and literature pointers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main Point: media can change expressed opinions without changing underlying attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: The media can change our (expressed) opinions without changing our (underlying) attitudes at all, through priming, framing, and agenda setting. Thus, political campaigns don't change our minds; they try to make us think about considerations that will lead us to support one candidate over another. The authors back up their arguments with experimental evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating media effects, distinguish short-term shifts in expressed opinions from deeper attitude change; look for experimental evidence to support causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priming
rubrics_metrics.description: Affects what you'll have at the top of your head when you make a judgment (see Zaller and Feldman 1992). So if the news covers poor economic performance, then leaps into an analysis of the president's performance, it's primed you to think poorly of the president.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priming operates by making certain considerations more accessible; use examples (e.g., economic coverage → negative presidential evaluations) and consult Zaller & Feldman (1992) for theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Media tells you how to think about something. Is it an indigenous rights issue, or an environmentalist story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing is about defining the lens through which an issue is perceived; compare to advocacy/network framing (e.g., Keck and Sikkink's TANs) when assessing how media shape interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-setting effects
rubrics_metrics.description: There's a 'lead story' effect. If you see prominent place given to unemployment stories (early, long stories in a broadcast), you pay more attention to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the prominence (position, length, repetition) of coverage as a predictor of public attention; however, interpret findings cautiously because of endogeneity (media select stories that will interest the public).

rubrics_metrics.name: Endogeneity caveat when attributing media influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveat: Endogeneity. The media tries to select stories that will interest the public. So although the media can set the agenda doesn't mean they necessarily do--it's endogenous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should account for selection effects and reverse causality when claiming media causally shape public priorities; employ designs that address endogeneity where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of experimental evidence to support causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors back up their arguments with experimental evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological implication: strengthen causal inferences about priming/framing/agenda-setting with experimental designs (or other identification strategies) rather than relying solely on observational correlations.
